title: Two decisions inside a repetition
goal: Follow the order of operations, trace an accumulator and test the loop boundary.

sections.title: Sequencing is ordered execution
paragraphs: In a simple program, reading input comes before computation and printing. Reordering these steps may use an uninitialized or outdated result.
Record the values that exist after each statement to reason about execution precisely.
Read n → set the sum to 0 → visit values → print the sum. Move the print before the loop and it shows the initial zero even when the later loop calculates correctly.

sections.title: Conditions select an alternative
paragraphs: if executes its body when its condition is true; else handles the alternative. n%2==0 tests whether an integer is even.
Test both outcomes. Inclusive and exclusive comparisons behave differently at the boundary.
The choice comes after reading. Input 8 takes the even branch and 7 takes the other one. A loop repeats that choice for each k.

sections.title: Loops describe repeated operations
paragraphs: To sum even values from 1 to n, we visit each k and add it to sum only if it is even. A loop avoids manually repeating similar statements.
for groups initialization, continuation and update. With while, updating the counter normally belongs in the loop body.
Separate two tests. k <= n permits another iteration, while k % 2 == 0 decides whether that iteration changes the sum. At k=3 the loop continues without adding anything.

sections.title: A trace reveals state
paragraphs: Sum the even numbers through 5. The counter also visits odd values. Which iterations change the sum?
Record the sum after each k, then reveal the trace.

reveal.title: Compare your prediction and trace the steps
paragraphs: At n=5, k visits 1 through 5. The sum changes at k=2 and k=4, reaching 6.
Write (k,sum) after each iteration. The invariant says that sum contains precisely the processed even integers.

tables.caption: How the sum changes with n = 5

sections.title: Termination and input bounds
paragraphs: Without advancing k, a loop guarded by k<=n may not terminate. Huge inputs can also consume time or overflow an integer.
Our exercise limits n to 0..10000, where the sum fits a 32-bit int. Broader programs must choose appropriate bounds and types.
For n=5 the next k after the final iteration is 6, so the test is false. For every allowed n the counter increases until it leaves the range.

sections.title: Zero iterations and the loop boundary
paragraphs: In for (int k=1; k<=n; ++k), initialization happens once, the condition is checked before each iteration, and ++k runs after the body. For n=0, the condition is false immediately and the sum stays 0. For n=6, 6 is included: 2+4+6=12. Replacing <= with < loses the last item when it is even. The parity check inside the body does not replace the loop condition.

sections.title: Input policy and execution limits
paragraphs: Integer inputs must fit the Code Studio int type. Failed extraction (text instead of a number or end of input) produces invalid; no further calculation is performed.

Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

sections.title: Try a separate task
paragraphs: Sum multiples of three from 1 through n inclusive. Accept integers n from 0 to 10000, otherwise print invalid. For n = 0 the sum is zero. Use a loop with a filter so its state can be traced.
Predict the first case and one boundary case. Practice has a separate starter. After running it, explain which check or operation produced each result.

selfcheck.prompt: For n = 6, trace the final iteration. What does the program print?
feedback: That is the result for n = 5 or the incorrect condition k < n.
21 sums every value, but the filter skips the odd ones.

practice.title: Sum of multiples of three
practice.task: Sum multiples of three from 1 through n inclusive. Accept integers n from 0 to 10000, otherwise print invalid. For n = 0 the sum is zero. Use a loop with a filter so its state can be traced.
criteria: Advance the counter every iteration, including when nothing is added.
Include n and return 0 for the empty range.
Explain why the sum changes only at k = 3 and k = 6 for n = 7.
practice.hint: Compare n = 5 and n = 6. Only the latter range contains 6.

steps.action: Check n = 0, 5, 6, 7 and the input bounds.
